title: Dental caries misinformation on Instagram: Investigation of sharing and engagement factors
screen_reason: Infodemiology content analysis of 500 Brazilian Portuguese Instagram posts about dental caries (published Aug 2018-Aug 2022, retrieved with CrowdTangle). Two trained, calibrated investigators coded each post's facticity against current scientific evidence; 109 of 500 posts (21.8%) contained misinformation. That is a share of items in a sample coded false/misleading against an external evidence base, with a stated denominator.

estimates.country: Brazil (Brazilian Portuguese posts; four posts from non-native Portuguese-speaking countries were excluded)
estimates.date: Posts published August 2018 - August 2022; dataset downloaded from CrowdTangle on 26 October 2022
estimates.measure_type: % of the most-interacted Brazilian Portuguese dental-caries Instagram posts that contained misinformation
estimates.denominator: 500 Instagram posts in Brazilian Portuguese about dental caries - the highest-total-interaction eligible posts, reached by manually screening 1,991 Portuguese-language posts from a CrowdTangle pull of 21,210 posts (7 caries search terms), after excluding 1,418 duplicates, 36 inaccessible links, 33 posts unrelated to dental caries and 4 posts from non-native Portuguese-speaking countries
estimates.definition: A post entered the numerator only if it unequivocally presented false or misleading information with the potential to harm Instagram users, judged against current scientific evidence on dental caries management (clinical guidelines, expert consensus statements and systematic reviews). Examples of coded misinformation: guava seeds growing inside a decayed tooth; killing caries- and tuberculosis-causing bacteria by ingesting cashew seed; herbs, cashew seeds and coconut oil as caries prevention or treatment
estimates.misinfo_def: "The term 'misinformation' was used to encompass false or misleading content, with or without the intention to cause harm. Thus, it incorporates both types of information disorders: misinformation per se and disinformation."
estimates.source_quote: The findings indicated that 21.8% of the analyzed posts contained misinformation, primarily on content shared by regular users regarding dental caries treatment.
estimates.page_loc: Abstract (quoted); same figure in Table 1, Facticity row ('Misinformation 109 (21.8)') and repeated in the Discussion, p. 7
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two independent investigators, comprehensively trained and calibrated on 50 randomly selected posts until inter-examiner agreement exceeded ICC 0.7; achieved ICC values of 0.84-0.96 across all coded parameters; disagreements resolved by joint consensus review. Facticity assessed against current scientific evidence including guidelines, consensus statements and systematic reviews on dental caries management. Reliability is reported as ICC, not kappa
estimates.moderator_quote: On October 26, 2022, a dataset containing 21,210 posts published between August 2018 and August 2022 was downloaded in .csv format using the following search terms: ["cárie dentária," "cárie," "caries," "lesão cariosa," "dente cariado," "lesões cariosas," "lesão de cárie"]. [...] Posts were ranked according to their total interaction. [...] To select the 500 most relevant posts based on total interaction, two independent investigators conducted a manual assessment, ensuring that only posts meeting the inclusion criteria were selected.
estimates.notes: ENGAGEMENT-RANKED denominator: the 500 posts are the top posts by total interaction out of 21,210 retrieved, so this is the prevalence of misinformation among the most-engaged caries posts, not among all caries posts - hence denom_selection=curated. That selection is likely to bias the estimate upward, since the paper itself finds misinformation posts had significantly higher median total interaction (4,654 vs 3,274; p < 0.001). Numerator is strict in one respect (misinformation had to be 'unequivocal' and potentially harmful) and broad in another (false OR misleading), so breadth is coded 'misleading'. Reliability is reported as ICC 0.84-0.96, which is a reasonable substitute for kappa on categorical codes but is not the conventional statistic. Note the 4 excluded posts from non-native-Portuguese countries imply the corpus could in principle include other Portuguese-speaking countries, but the paper frames the corpus as Brazilian Portuguese throughout.

missed_or_uncertain: NOT extracted, with reasons. (1) NO engagement-weighted (SHARING) row is possible: Table 1 gives only MEDIAN total interaction by facticity (misinformation 4,654 [2,961, 8,697] vs information 3,274 [2,664, 5,408], p < 0.001) and median overperforming scores (1.71 vs 2.09, p = 0.070). Medians are not shares and no interaction totals are printed, so the share of all interactions that went to misinformation cannot be derived without violating R8. This is the paper's central engagement claim and it stays unusable for prevalence purposes. (2) NO subgroup misinformation shares are reported. The association between misinformation and author type or content type is given only as GSEM odds ratios (misinformation negatively associated with business/health profiles, OR = 0.22, p < 0.001; positively associated with treatment content, OR = 2.11, p = 0.007), never as a share of posts within each profile type, so a by-profile row cannot be built. (3) Other Table 1 distributions are not falsity measures: business/health profiles 299 (59.8%), regular users 201 (40.2%); financial motivation 403 (80.6%); positive sentiment 274 (54.8%); treatment content 328 (65.6%), prevention 172 (34.4%); photo/album 452 (90.4%), link/video 48 (9.6%); median publication age 685 days. (4) Topic-modelling results (Tables 3 and 4: misinformation topics = caries treatment, diet, oral hygiene, microorganisms; accurate-information topics = prevention, oral hygiene, treatment, with coherence and eigenvalues) report no shares. (5) Remaining GSEM paths, model fit (AIC 4,522.40; BIC 4,657.27) and all Mann-Whitney comparisons are associations, not prevalence. (6) Minor internal inconsistency worth an adjudicator's eye: the Study design section says normality and homogeneity were assessed with Shapiro-Wilk and Levene, while the Statistical analysis section says Kolmogorov-Smirnov and Levene. It does not affect the extracted value.

rob.design: Retrospective infodemiology content analysis reported per STROBE; no human participants, ethics approval not required (public data), de-identified data on Figshare. CrowdTangle (Meta) pull on 26 October 2022 of 21,210 Instagram posts published August 2018-August 2022 matching seven Portuguese caries keywords, with post metadata including total interaction (likes + comments + views) and CrowdTangle's overperforming score. Posts were ranked by total interaction and manually screened down the ranking: 1,991 Portuguese-language posts assessed, 1,418 duplicates, 36 inaccessible links, 33 off-topic posts and 4 posts from non-native Portuguese-speaking countries excluded, leaving the 500 analysed posts. Two independent investigators, trained and calibrated on 50 random posts to an ICC > 0.7 threshold (achieved ICC 0.84-0.96 across author profile, content, motivation, facticity, format and sentiment), coded all posts; disagreements resolved by joint consensus. Posts were rendered to PDF so different researchers could code independently at different times. Facticity judged against guidelines, consensus statements and systematic reviews. Analysis: Mann-Whitney U tests and GSEM path analysis grounded in the Theory of Planned Behavior. Author-stated limitations: Portuguese-only corpus limits cultural generalization; no user demographics; sample size limited by manual coding. Not stated but material: the denominator is engagement-ranked, not a random sample, and no confidence interval is given for the 21.8%.
rob.item6_quote: The facticity of the content was evaluated against current scientific evidence, including guidelines, consensus statements, and systematic reviews related to dental caries management. 22-24 A post was considered to contain misinformation only if it unequivocally presented false or misleading information with the potential to harm Instagram users.
